import os, shutil, pathlib

original_dir = pathlib.Path("C://Users//Alienware//Downloads//catsndogs//data//train//train")
new_base_dir = pathlib.Path("../data/kaggle_dogs_vs_cats_small")

def make_subset(subset_name, start_index, end_index):
    for category in ("cat", "dog"):
        dir = new_base_dir / subset_name / category
        os.makedirs(dir)
        fnames = [f"{category}.{i}.jpg" for i in range(start_index, end_index)]
        for fname in fnames:
            shutil.copyfile(src=original_dir / fname,
                            dst=dir / fname)

make_subset("train", start_index=0, end_index=1000)
make_subset("validation", start_index=1000, end_index=1500)
make_subset("test", start_index=1500, end_index=2500)

def plot_images(path, n=5):
    files = os.listdir(path)[:n]  # Take the first n files
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, n, figsize=(15, 5))

        img = Image.open(os.path.join(path, file))
        axs[i].imshow(img)
        axs[i].axis("off")
    plt.show()

import tensorflow as tf  # ensure TensorFlow is imported

# image statistics
def analyze_image_statistics(dataset):
    pixel_mean = []
    pixel_std = []
    # The dataset yields (images, labels)
    for images, _ in dataset:
        pixel_mean.append(tf.reduce_mean(images))
        pixel_std.append(tf.math.reduce_std(images))
    
    return {
        'mean': tf.reduce_mean(pixel_mean),
        'std': tf.reduce_mean(pixel_std)
    }

# Use the dataset object obtained from image_dataset_from_directory
stats = analyze_image_statistics(train_dataset)
print("\nImage Statistics:")
print(f"Mean pixel value: {stats['mean']:.2f}")
print(f"Std pixel value: {stats['std']:.2f}")

# class names
class_names = train_dataset.class_names
print("\nClass names:", class_names)

# image counts
def count_images_per_class(dataset):
    counts = {name: 0 for name in class_names}
    for images, labels in dataset:
        for label in labels:
            counts[class_names[label.numpy()]] += 1
    return counts

3 Train two networks¶

3.1 Define a Neural Network - Convnet From Scratch¶

Definning the model¶

In [32]:
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow import keras
from tensorflow.keras import layers

# Define the input
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(180, 180, 3))

# Rescaling the image pixels (normalization)
x = layers.Rescaling(1./255)(inputs)

# First convolutional layer (32 filters, 3x3 kernel, ReLU activation)
x = layers.Conv2D(filters=32, kernel_size=3, activation="relu")(x)
x = layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2)(x)

# Second convolutional layer (64 filters, 3x3 kernel, ReLU activation)
x = layers.Conv2D(filters=64, kernel_size=3, activation="relu")(x)
x = layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2)(x)

# Third convolutional layer (128 filters, 3x3 kernel, ReLU activation)
x = layers.Conv2D(filters=128, kernel_size=3, activation="relu")(x)
x = layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2)(x)

# Fourth convolutional layer (256 filters, 3x3 kernel, ReLU activation)
x = layers.Conv2D(filters=256, kernel_size=3, activation="relu")(x)
x = layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2)(x)

# Flatten layer to convert 2D matrix to a 1D vector
x = layers.Flatten()(x)

# Dropout layer to prevent overfitting (regularization)
x = layers.Dropout(0.5)(x)

# Output layer with 1 neuron (binary classification) and sigmoid activation
outputs = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")(x)

# Create the model
model = keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs)

# Display the model summary
model.summary()

3.2.2 Fast feature extraction without data augmentation¶

Extracting the VGG16 features and corresponding labels

Note: running the following cell on a CPU will take about 10 minutes

In [40]:
import numpy as np

def get_features_and_labels(dataset):
    all_features = []
    all_labels = []
    for images, labels in dataset:
        preprocessed_images = keras.applications.vgg16.preprocess_input(images)
        features = conv_base.predict(preprocessed_images)
        all_features.append(features)
        all_labels.append(labels)
    return np.concatenate(all_features), np.concatenate(all_labels)

train_features, train_labels =  get_features_and_labels(train_dataset)
val_features, val_labels =  get_features_and_labels(validation_dataset)
test_features, test_labels =  get_features_and_labels(test_dataset)

Defining and training the densely connected classifier

Here we define a new dense neural networks, of only two (neuronal/trainable) layers.

In [42]:
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(5, 5, 512))
x = layers.Flatten()(inputs)
x = layers.Dense(256)(x)
x = layers.Dropout(0.5)(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
acc = history.history["accuracy"]

Adding a data augmentation stage and a classifier to the convolutional base

In [50]:
data_augmentation = keras.Sequential(
    [
        layers.RandomFlip("horizontal"),
        layers.RandomRotation(0.1),
        layers.RandomZoom(0.2),
    ]
)

inputs = keras.Input(shape=(180, 180, 3))
x = data_augmentation(inputs)
x = keras.applications.vgg16.preprocess_input(x)
x = conv_base(x)
x = layers.Flatten()(x)
x = layers.Dense(256)(x)
x = layers.Dropout(0.5)(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)

4.2 Confusion matrix , classification_report, precision_recall_curve¶

In [63]:
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve, classification_report, confusion_matrix
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Load the best models
from tensorflow.keras.models import load_model

convnet_model = load_model("./models/convnet_from_scratch.keras")
feature_extraction_model = load_model("./models/feature_extraction.keras")
feature_extraction_aug_model = load_model("./models/feature_extraction_with_data_augmentation.keras")
fine_tuned_model = load_model("./models/fine_tuning.keras")

# Predictions and evaluation
def evaluate_model(model, dataset, true_labels, dataset_type="test_dataset"):
    print(f"\nEvaluating model on {dataset_type}:")
    # Get predictions (probabilities)
    if dataset_type == "test_dataset":
        probs = model.predict(dataset).ravel()
    else:  # test_features and test_labels
        probs = model.predict(dataset).ravel()
    preds = np.round(probs)  # Convert to binary labels
    
    # Classification metrics
    print("Confusion Matrix:")
    print(confusion_matrix(true_labels, preds))
    print("\nClassification Report:")
    print(classification_report(true_labels, preds))
    
    # Precision-Recall curve
    precision, recall, _ = precision_recall_curve(true_labels, probs)
    plt.plot(recall, precision, label=f"{dataset_type} - Precision-Recall")
    plt.xlabel("Recall")
    plt.ylabel("Precision")
    plt.title(f"Precision-Recall Curve - {dataset_type}")
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()

# Evaluate each model

# ConvNet from Scratch
evaluate_model(convnet_model, test_dataset, test_labels, "ConvNet")

# Feature Extraction
evaluate_model(feature_extraction_model, test_features, test_labels, "Feature Extraction")

# Feature Extraction with Data Augmentation
evaluate_model(feature_extraction_aug_model, test_dataset, test_labels, "Feature Extraction with Augmentation")

# Fine-Tuning
evaluate_model(fine_tuned_model, test_dataset, test_labels, "Fine-Tuned Model")

Conclusion¶

Data and Setup¶

  • Dataset Distribution:
    • Training set: 1000 cat images and 1000 dog images.
    • Validation set: 500 cat images and 500 dog images.
    • Test set: 1000 cat images and 1000 dog images.
  • Image Statistics:
    • Mean pixel value: 114.03
    • Standard deviation: 65.50
    These metrics are fundamental for understanding the preprocessing and normalization needs.

Model Performance Overview¶

1. Custom ConvNet Architecture¶

  • Test Accuracy: 74.6%
  • Confusion Matrix:
    • Class 0: 796 correctly classified, 204 misclassified.
    • Class 1: 696 correctly classified, 304 misclassified.
  • Classification Report:
    • Class 0: Precision = 0.72, Recall = 0.80, F1-score ≈ 0.76
    • Class 1: Precision = 0.77, Recall = 0.70, F1-score ≈ 0.73
  • Insight:
    This baseline model shows a relatively high rate of misclassifications, indicating that a simple architecture does not capture the complex features as effectively.

2. VGG16 using Feature Extraction¶

  • Test Accuracy: 96.3%
  • Confusion Matrix:
    • Significantly fewer misclassifications (only 44 and 30 errors for the two classes).
  • Classification Report:
    • Both classes have precision and recall values in the range of 0.96–0.97, with F1-scores around 0.96.
  • Insight:
    Leveraging a pre-trained model via feature extraction dramatically improves performance by utilizing learned representations from larger datasets.

3. VGG16 with Data Augmentation (Feature Extraction)¶

  • Test Accuracy: 97%
  • Confusion Matrix:
    • Further reduction in errors: One class shows 979 correct vs. 21 errors, and the other 966 correct vs. 34 errors.
  • Classification Report:
    • Both classes exhibit slight improvements in precision and recall (approximately 0.97–0.98), which leads to balanced performance.
  • Insight:
    Data augmentation aids in improving generalization, which reduces overfitting and slightly enhances overall accuracy.

4. Fine-Tuned VGG16 Model¶

  • Test Accuracy: 97.8%
  • Confusion Matrix:
    • Best performance with only 22 and 23 misclassifications for classes 0 and 1, respectively.
  • Classification Report:
    • Both classes achieve precision, recall, and F1-scores of approximately 0.98.
  • Insight:
    Fine-tuning the pre-trained VGG16 network allows it to adapt more closely to the specific features of the dataset, resulting in the highest accuracy and best balanced performance across all metrics.

Final Conclusion and Recommendations¶

  • Comparison of Approaches:
    • The custom ConvNet reached a 74.6% accuracy, substantially lower than models leveraging transfer learning.
    • Among the VGG16-based models, there is a clear performance hierarchy:
      1. Feature Extraction: 96.3% accuracy.
      2. Feature Extraction with Augmentation: 97% accuracy.
      3. Fine-Tuned VGG16: 97.8% accuracy.
  • Key Performance Metrics:
    • Accuracy: Improved from 74.6% (ConvNet) to 97.8% (Fine-Tuned VGG16).
    • Precision, Recall, F1-Score: The fine-tuned model shows balanced metrics (all around 0.98), indicating reliable classification for both classes.
    • Confusion Matrix: A clear reduction in false positives and false negatives is observed as the model complexity increases, especially with fine-tuning.
